questions.q: Fill up: The fenestration slits of the capillary endothelium with fenestrations are ______ in diameter.
questions.exp: Fenestration slits: 50–100 nm diameter (30–50 nm belongs to the podocyte filtration slits). (Book p730)

questions.q: Fill up: The endothelial fenestrations are coated with ______, whose negative charge repels negatively charged proteins.
questions.exp: Coated with podocalyxin → −ve charge repels negatively charged proteins; heparan sulfate proteoglycans belong to the GBM. (Book p730)

questions.q: The function of the fenestrated capillary endothelium is to prevent proteinuria (albuminuria) and thereby prevent:
questions.exp: Function: prevent proteinuria (albuminuria) → prevent nephrotoxicity. (Book p730)

questions.q: All of the following are described with the capillary-endothelium disease PSGN EXCEPT:
opts: Exudative neutrophilic infiltration of the lumen
questions.exp: PSGN (capillary endothelium disease): microhematuria, minimal proteinuria, exudative neutrophilic infiltration of lumen — not nephrotic-range proteinuria. (Book p730)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about PSGN as an endothelial disease is TRUE?
opts: It carries no risk for CKD
It carries a high risk of progression to CKD
questions.exp: Disease of capillary endothelium (PSGN): microhematuria, minimal proteinuria, exudative neutrophilic infiltration, no risk for CKD. (Book p730)

questions.q: PSGN, the disease of the capillary endothelium, stands for:
questions.exp: PSGN = Post Streptococcal Glomerulo Nephritis, the capillary-endothelium disease. (Book p730)

questions.q: Which sequence matches the book's pathophysiology of CKD chain?
opts: ↓ functional nephrons → hyperfiltration by remaining nephrons → intraglomerular HTN → capillary stretching → proteinuria
Hyperfiltration → ↓ functional nephrons → proteinuria → intraglomerular HTN
Proteinuria → ↓ functional nephrons → hyperfiltration → capillary stretching
Intraglomerular HTN → ↓ functional nephrons → hyperfiltration → proteinuria
questions.exp: ↓ number of functional nephrons → hyperfiltration by remaining nephrons → intraglomerular hypertension → stretching of capillaries with ↑ pore diameter → proteinuria. (Book p730)

questions.q: Fill up: Stretching of glomerular capillaries in the CKD chain increases the capillary ______ diameter.
questions.exp: Stretching of capillaries → ↑ capillary pore diameter → proteinuria (albuminuria). (Book p730)

questions.q: Fill up: Proteinuria causes tubulotoxicity and interstitial inflammation, with formation of TGF-______.
questions.exp: Interstitial inflammation → TGF-β formation → tubulo-interstitial fibrosis. (Book p730)

questions.q: The terminal step of the CKD pathophysiology flowchart after TGF-β formation is:
questions.exp: TGF-β formation → tubulo-interstitial fibrosis closes the chain. (Book p730)

questions.q: By the size rule, substances with an effective diameter above which value do NOT pass the filtration barrier?
questions.exp: Size: effective diameter < 4 mm passes through; > 8–10 mm doesn't pass. (Book p730)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the charge rule of the filtration barrier is TRUE?
opts: Molecules of effective diameter 4–8 mm are repelled if they carry a negative charge
Molecules of effective diameter 4–8 mm are repelled if positively charged
Charge plays no role between 4 and 8 mm
Only molecules above 10 mm are charge-repelled
questions.exp: Charge: effective diameter 4–8 mm is repelled if −ve charge (eg. albumin 7.6 mm, −vely charged). (Book p730)

questions.q: The book's charge-rule example, albumin, has an effective diameter of:
questions.exp: Eg: albumin 7.6 mm, −vely charged — hence repelled despite sitting in the 4–8 mm window. (Book p730)

questions.q: All of the following are labelled in the glomerular-capillary figure EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Figure labels: podocyte, glomerular basement membrane, foot processes, capillary, mesangial angle, capillary endothelium, microfilaments, mesangium and mesangial matrix; the slit diaphragm is diagrammed later with podocytes. (Book p730)

questions.q: The major constituent of the glomerular basement membrane is:
questions.exp: GBM constituent: type 4 collagen (majorly). (Book p731)

questions.q: Match each type-4 collagen configuration with its basement membrane — 1) α1 α1 α2 2) α3 α4 α5 3) α5 α5 α6 … A) Epidermal BM B) Present at birth C) GBM, cochlear BM and ocular BM
questions.exp: α1α1α2 at birth; α3α4α5 in GBM, cochlear BM and ocular BM; α5α5α6 in epidermal BM. (Book p731)

questions.q: A defect in type 4 collagen produces:
questions.exp: Type 4 collagen defect → Alport syndrome. (Book p731)

questions.q: Match each Alport syndrome form with its profile — 1) The 85% form 2) The 10–15% form … A) AD/AR inheritance, α3+/α4 defect, normal skin stain B) X-linked inheritance, α5 defect, absent skin stain
opts: Both are X-linked with absent stain
Both are AD/AR with normal stain
questions.exp: 85% X-linked with α5 defect and absent skin/epidermal immunofluorescence stain; 10–15% AD/AR with α3+/α4 defect and normal stain. (Book p731)

questions.q: Fill up: The negative charge of the GBM comes from heparin sulfate proteoglycans such as perlecan and ______.
questions.exp: Negative charge: heparin sulfate proteoglycans (eg: perlecan, agrin). (Book p731)

questions.q: Fill up: Under the light microscope the GBM is best seen with Gomori methenamine silver stain, preferred over Masson's ______.
questions.exp: Stains under light m/s: Gomori methenamine silver stain > Masson's trichrome. (Book p731)

questions.q: Normal GBM thickness on electron microscopy is:
questions.exp: Thickness: normal 350–400 nm; thin GBM disease < 200 nm. (Book p731)

questions.q: Thin GBM disease is defined by a GBM thickness of:
questions.exp: Thin GBM disease: < 200 nm against a normal 350–400 nm. (Book p731)

questions.q: All of the following are true of the GBM EXCEPT:
opts: Its negative charge comes from podocalyxin
Its major constituent is type 4 collagen
It can be visualised by electron microscopy
questions.exp: GBM negative charge = heparin sulfate proteoglycans (perlecan, agrin); podocalyxin coats the endothelial fenestrations and podocyte slits. (Book p731)

questions.q: The supporting cells of the filtration barrier named in the book's note are the:
questions.exp: Note: supporting cells of the filtration barrier = mesangial cells. (Book p731)

questions.q: Fill up: The constituent of mesangial cells listed in the note is ______.
questions.exp: Mesangial cell constituent: microfilaments. (Book p731)

questions.q: Fill up: Violent contraction of mesangial cells ruptures the capillary and causes ______.
questions.exp: Violent contraction → rupture of capillary → macrohematuria; it also ↓ surface area → ↓ GFR. (Book p731)

questions.q: Mesangial contraction reduces the capillary surface area and therefore:
questions.exp: ↓ surface area → ↓ GFR. (Book p731)

questions.q: Mesangial proliferative disease is defined by more than how many mesangial cells in a space?
questions.exp: Mesangial cell/mesangial proliferative = >3 mesangial cells in a space. (Book p731)

questions.q: The m/c prototype disease of mesangial cell/matrix expansion listed is:
questions.exp: Mesangial cell expansion (matrix expansion)/glomerular disease: IgA nephropathy (m/c) prototype disease. (Book p731)

questions.q: All of the following are labelled in the light-microscope image EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Light microscope image labels mesangial cells, Bowman's space, CL (capillary lumen), PT (proximal tubule) and open capillary loops; the macula densa appears in the JGA figure. (Book p731)

questions.q: Match each juxtaglomerular-apparatus figure label with its synonym — 1) JG cells 2) Lacis cells … A) Extraglomerular mesangial cells B) Granular cells
questions.exp: Figure: JG cells (granular cells); lacis cells (extraglomerular mesangial cells), with macula densa, AA, EA, PCT, DCT, parietal and visceral layers. (Book p731)

questions.q: The slit diaphragm / filtration slits are defined as the space between:
questions.exp: Slit diaphragm/filtration slits: space btw 2 podocytes. (Book p732)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about podocytes is TRUE?
opts: They are terminally differentiated and cannot be regenerated
They are the main filtration site of the GBM
They lie inside the capillary lumen
questions.exp: Podocytes: terminally differentiated cells (cannot be regenerated). (Book p732)

questions.q: Fill up: Podocytes are anchored to the GBM by their ______, where no filtration occurs.
questions.exp: Anchored to GBM by foot processes: no filtration at the anchor. (Book p732)

questions.q: Match each podocyte protein compartment with its proteins — 1) Inside 2) Surface … A) Podocin and TRPC6 B) α actinin 4
questions.exp: Proteins: inside = α actinin 4; surface = podocin and TRPC6. (Book p732)

questions.q: The diameter given for the podocyte filtration slits (coated with podocalyxin) is:
questions.exp: Diameter: 30–50 nm, coated with podocalyxin (endothelial fenestrations are 50–100 nm). (Book p732)

questions.q: All of the following are true of nephrins EXCEPT:
opts: They are the angiotensin II binding receptors of podocytes
They are proteins contained in the slit diaphragm
questions.exp: Nephrins: proteins in the slit diaphragm, prevent protein leak, maintain podocyte integrity; angiotensin binds a separate angiotensin II binding receptor on the podocyte. (Book p732)

questions.q: Fill up: In the slit-diaphragm podocyte figure, α3β1 integrin anchors the foot process to the GBM via laminin-______.
questions.exp: Figure (b): α3β1 integrin with laminin-11 links the podocyte foot process to the glomerular basement membrane. (Book p732)

questions.q: Angiotensin binding to the podocyte's angiotensin II binding receptor causes:
questions.exp: Angiotensin binds podocyte angiotensin II binding receptor → downregulation of nephrin. (Book p732)

questions.q: Fill up: Loss of podocyte integrity in this chain is termed ______.
questions.exp: Downregulation of nephrin → loss of podocyte integrity (podocytopathies). (Book p732)

questions.q: Which sequence matches the book's podocyte-loss chain?
opts: Podocyte detached → podocyturia → podocytopenia → GBM attaches to parietal cells → synechiae → glomerulosclerosis → CKD
Podocyturia → podocyte detached → podocytopenia → synechiae → CKD
questions.exp: Chain: podocyte detached → podocyturia → podocytopenia → GBM attaches to parietal epithelial cells → synechiae formation → glomerulosclerosis → CKD. (Book p732)

questions.q: Fill up: After podocytopenia the GBM attaches to parietal epithelial cells, producing ______ formation.
questions.exp: GBM attaches to parietal epithelial cells → synechiae formation → glomerulosclerosis. (Book p732)

questions.q: The last two steps of the podocyte-loss chain before CKD are synechiae formation followed by:
questions.exp: Synechiae formation → glomerulosclerosis → CKD. (Book p732)

questions.q: ARBs/ACE inhibitors are used in the Rx of diabetic nephropathy in order to:
opts: Block the angiotensin II receptor on podocytes
questions.exp: ARBs/ACEI(−)s used in Rx of diabetic nephropathy to block the angiotensin II receptor (preventing nephrin downregulation). (Book p732)

questions.q: In congenital nephrotic syndrome, DMS stands for:
questions.exp: Congenital nephrotic syndrome: DMS = diffuse mesangial sclerosis. (Book p733)

questions.q: Match each congenital nephrotic syndrome type with its defect and age — 1) Finnish type 2) Podocin type 3) Autosomal dominant type … A) α actinin 4/TRPC6 defect at adolescence B) Nephrin (NPHS1) defect at birth C) Podocin defect at 3–5 years
questions.exp: Finnish type: AR, nephrin NPHS1, birth; podocin type: AR, podocin, 3–5 years; AD type: α actinin 4/TRPC6, adolescence. (Book p733)

questions.q: Fill up: The outcome of Finnish type nephrotic syndrome is 100% ______.
questions.exp: Finnish type: outcome 100% mortality, histology ≡ DMS, management dash. (Book p733)

questions.q: Fill up: Both the podocin type and the autosomal dominant type show 100% steroid resistance progressing to ______, with histology ≡ FSGS.
questions.exp: Podocin and AD types: 100% steroid resistance → CKD, ≡ FSGS, managed by renal transplant. (Book p733)

questions.q: Finnish type nephrotic syndrome is m/c seen in:
opts: Premature babies with a large placenta
questions.exp: Finnish type nephrotic syndrome m/c seen in premature babies with large placenta. (Book p733)

questions.q: Besides congenital nephrotic syndrome, DMS is also seen in:
questions.exp: Note: DMS also seen in Denys-Drash syndrome. (Book p733)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the congenital nephrotic syndrome table is TRUE?
opts: The Finnish type shows histology ≡ DMS with no management listed
The Finnish type responds fully to steroids
The podocin type presents at birth with 100% mortality
The autosomal dominant type has histology ≡ DMS
questions.exp: Finnish type: ≡ DMS, management '–'; podocin and AD types are ≡ FSGS with steroid resistance → CKD and renal transplant. (Book p733)

questions.q: Match each filtration-barrier site with its disease — 1) Endothelium 2) GBM 3) Mesangium … A) Alport B) PSGN C) IgA nephropathy
questions.exp: Site–disease: endothelium = PSGN; GBM = Alport; mesangium = IgA nephropathy. (Book p733)

questions.q: All of the following sit under 'podocyte with podocytopenia' EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Podocyte with podocytopenia: diabetes, FSGS, membranous; MCD sits under podocyte without podocytopenia. (Book p733)

questions.q: The disease listed under 'podocyte without podocytopenia' is:
questions.exp: Without podocytopenia: MCD. (Book p733)

questions.q: Which of the following site–disease pairings is TRUE as written in the book?
questions.exp: The table pairs GBM with Alport, endothelium with PSGN and mesangium with IgA nephropathy. (Book p733)

questions.q: Fill up: In the site–disease table, the endothelial site corresponds to the disease ______.
questions.exp: Endothelium → PSGN in the site–disease table. (Book p733)
